mcqs.question: Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes heat from work?

options.A: Heat is energy transferred due to a temperature difference, whereas work is energy transferred when a force acts through a displacement.
options.B: Heat is energy transferred when a force acts through a displacement, whereas work is energy transferred due to a temperature difference.
options.C: Both heat and work are transferred only when there is a change in the internal energy of a system.
options.D: Heat and work are identical concepts; the terms are used interchangeably in thermodynamics.

mcqs.answer: Heat is energy transferred due to a temperature difference, whereas work is energy transferred when a force acts through a displacement.
mcqs.explanation: Heat refers to energy transfer caused solely by a temperature gradient, while work refers to energy transfer caused by macroscopic forces causing displacement (e.g., piston movement). Options B, C, and D are incorrect because they reverse the definitions or conflate the two distinct modes of energy transfer.

mcqs.question: In the sign convention commonly used in thermodynamics, what sign is assigned to the work done by the system on its surroundings during an expansion?

options.D: It depends on the type of gas

mcqs.explanation: The standard thermodynamic sign convention takes work done by the system as negative because the system loses energy. Work done on the system is taken as positive. Therefore, during expansion (system does work), the work term is negative. Options A, C, and D are incorrect.

mcqs.learning_point: Calculate work in simple thermodynamic processes
mcqs.question: A gas expands isobarically at a constant pressure of 2.0 × 10^5 Pa from an initial volume of 1.0 × 10^-3 m³ to a final volume of 3.0 × 10^-3 m³. What is the work done by the gas?
mcqs.explanation: Work in an isobaric process is W = PΔV. ΔV = 3.0×10^-3 – 1.0×10^-3 = 2.0×10^-3 m³. Thus, W = (2.0×10^5 Pa)(2.0×10^-3 m³) = 4.0×10^2 J = 400 J. Option B is correct; the other values arise from arithmetic errors.

mcqs.question: On a pressure‑volume (P‑V) diagram, which of the following curves represents the greatest amount of work done by the system?

options.A: A vertical line at constant volume.
options.B: A horizontal line at constant pressure extending from V₁ to V₂.
options.C: A curve that returns to its initial point, forming a closed loop.
options.D: A sloping line that connects the same initial and final volumes but at a lower pressure than the horizontal line.

mcqs.answer: A horizontal line at constant pressure extending from V₁ to V₂.
mcqs.explanation: Work equals the area under the curve on a P‑V diagram. A horizontal line at constant pressure encloses a rectangular area (P × ΔV), which is larger than the area under a vertical line (zero work) or a lower‑pressure sloping line. A closed loop represents net zero work over a cycle. Hence option B is correct.

mcqs.question: A sealed cylinder contains an ideal gas. In case (i) the gas is heated at constant volume, and in case (ii) the gas is compressed slowly by a piston while being thermally insulated. Which statement correctly describes the energy transfer in each case?

options.A: Case (i) involves work only; case (ii) involves heat only.
options.B: Both cases involve only heat transfer.
options.C: Case (i) involves heat transfer only; case (ii) involves work only.
options.D: Both cases involve both heat and work.

mcqs.answer: Case (i) involves heat transfer only; case (ii) involves work only.
mcqs.explanation: At constant volume, the gas cannot do boundary work, so the increase in internal energy comes solely from heat added (case i). When the gas is compressed adiabatically (thermally insulated), no heat is exchanged; the energy change is due to work done on the gas (case ii). Options A, B, and D misattribute the modes of energy transfer.

mcqs.question: A gas expands against a constant external pressure of 1.5 × 10^5 Pa, increasing its volume from 2.0 × 10^-3 m³ to 5.0 × 10^-3 m³. According to the thermodynamic sign convention, what is the sign of the work term (W) in the first‑law equation ΔU = Q + W?

options.D: It can be either positive or negative depending on the heat flow

mcqs.explanation: During expansion, the system does work on the surroundings, so W is negative in the convention ΔU = Q + W. The magnitude is W = –PΔV = –(1.5×10^5 Pa)(3.0×10^-3 m³) = –450 J. Hence the sign is negative. Options A, C, and D are incorrect.

mcqs.learning_point: Calculate work in simple thermodynamic processes
mcqs.question: A student claims: "In any thermodynamic process, the work done on the system is always taken as positive, irrespective of the sign convention used in the textbook." Which part of this statement is a misconception?

options.A: Work done on the system can be negative in the physics sign convention.
options.B: Work done on the system is always zero because only heat changes internal energy.
options.C: The magnitude of work does not depend on the process path.
options.D: All textbooks use the same sign convention for work.

mcqs.answer: Work done on the system can be negative in the physics sign convention.
mcqs.explanation: Different disciplines adopt different sign conventions. In many physics contexts, work done by the system is taken as positive, making work done on the system negative. Therefore, the blanket statement that work done on the system is always positive is incorrect. Options B, C, and D are unrelated misconceptions.

mcqs.question: Two processes are shown on a P‑V diagram. Process A is a straight line from (P₁, V₁) to (P₂, V₂). Process B follows the same endpoints but first moves horizontally to (P₁, V₂) and then vertically down to (P₂, V₂). Which process does more work and why?

options.A: Process A does more work because a slanted line always encloses a larger area than a rectangular path.
options.B: Process B does more work because the horizontal segment at higher pressure contributes the greatest area.
options.C: Both processes do the same amount of work because they have identical initial and final states.
options.D: Neither process does any work because work depends only on temperature change.

mcqs.answer: Process B does more work because the horizontal segment at higher pressure contributes the greatest area.
mcqs.explanation: Work equals the area under the curve. In Process B, the horizontal segment at pressure P₁ (the higher of the two pressures) spans the full volume change, giving an area P₁·(V₂‑V₁). The subsequent vertical drop adds no area. In Process A, the average pressure is (P₁+P₂)/2, so the area is ((P₁+P₂)/2)·(V₂‑V₁), which is smaller because P₂ < P₁. Hence Process B does more work. Option C is wrong because work is path‑dependent; option D misstates the definition of work; option A incorrectly assumes a slanted line gives larger area.
